written.q: Define reinforcement learning and contrast it with supervised and unsupervised learning. Give two real examples.
written.a: RL: an agent learns by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback as rewards (+) or penalties (−). Supervised learning has correct answers (teacher), unsupervised has no answers (find groups), RL has only a reward or penalty after it acts, which may come later. Examples: a puppy trained with treats; Boston Dynamics robots learning movements; game-playing programs; chatbots tuned with human-feedback rewards.

written.q: Define agent, environment, state, action, reward, policy and episode, and explain pi(s, a<sub>i</sub>) = P<sub>i</sub> with an example.
written.a: Agent: the learner that acts; environment: everything it interacts with; state s: current situation; action a: what it does; reward r: feedback number after an action; policy π: rule for choosing actions; episode: one full try from start to end. π(s, ai) = Pi means in state s the policy chooses action ai with probability Pi, and the probabilities for the state add to 1. Example: π(s1, lift leg) = 0.7, π(s1, turn) = 0.2, π(s1, wait) = 0.1.

written.q: Explain the return and discount factor. In the corridor A-B-C with +10 at C, compute G for rewards 0, 0, 10 with γ = 0.9 and 0.5, and V(A) and V(B) for γ = 0.9.
written.a: Return G = r1 + γr2 + γ²r3 + …, the total reward over time, with later rewards worth less (γ between 0 and 1; near 1 patient, near 0 short-sighted). γ = 0.9: 0.81 × 10 = 8.1; γ = 0.5: 0.25 × 10 = 2.5. Under always-go-right: V(B) = 10, V(A) = 0.9 × 10 = 9.

written.q: Explain exploration vs exploitation and compute the ε-greedy probabilities for ε = 0.3 and three actions.
written.a: Exploit: use the action that has worked best; explore: try something different that may be better. ε-greedy explores with probability ε (random action) and exploits otherwise. With ε = 0.3 and 3 actions, exploration gives 0.3/3 = 0.1 to each action; the best action gets 0.7 + 0.1 = 0.8; the others 0.1 each (total 1.0). Often ε starts large and shrinks.

written.q: State the Q-learning update and perform the first two episodes in the corridor (α = 0.5, γ = 0.9, Q = 0 initially, +10 at C).
written.a: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max Q(s′,a′) − Q(s,a)]. Episode 1: Q(A,right) = 0 + 0.5[0 + 0 − 0] = 0; Q(B,right) = 0 + 0.5[10 − 0] = 5. Episode 2: Q(A,right) = 0 + 0.5[0 + 0.9×5 − 0] = 2.25; Q(B,right) = 5 + 0.5[10 − 5] = 7.5. Reward information spreads backward from the goal toward the true values 10 and 9.

written.q: Explain policy gradients using the fries story.
written.a: Ordinary backpropagation needs the correct answer, which RL lacks. Policy gradients: use the network to decide (hunger 0: P(Norm's) = P(Squatch's) = 0.5; a random number 0.2 picks Squatch's); guess that this was right and compute the derivative (0.5); get the reward from the environment (small portion when not hungry: +1.0); multiply the derivative by the reward (0.5); take a gradient-descent step (learning rate 1.0 × 0.5 = 0.5). A positive reward makes the guessed action more likely; a negative reward flips the sign and makes it less likely.

written.q: Explain reward hacking and two other practical problems of RL.
written.a: Reward hacking: the agent finds a cheat that earns reward without doing what was meant (a cleaning robot rewarded for no visible dirt hides dirt under a rug), so the reward must match the real goal. Other problems: lots of trial and error (millions of tries; costly or risky in the real world), safe exploration (random actions can cause harm), delayed reward and credit assignment, and policies that are hard to explain.
